::: {.content-visible when-format="docx"}
# Book_28 — Privileged Access Management
:::


::: {.callout-note}
Active Directory's approach to privileged access was one of the worst-kept secrets in federal IT: the controls existed on paper and on a network diagram, but in practice, privileged group membership crept over years, domain admin counts exceeded audit thresholds, and service account credentials rotated on someone's personal calendar reminder. Migration forces the reckoning. This book traces each implicit PAM dependency AD carried — the shared credential vault that never was, the elevated session that never logged, the service account that never rotated — and maps the governed replacements: Entra PIM for time-bounded JIT elevation, CyberArk Privilege Cloud as the vault and session broker, CPM for automated credential rotation, and PSM for tamper-evident session recording. Every mechanism is OrgPath-addressed, HRIT-grounded, and governed under the L0–L4 actuation ladder.
:::

## Companion canon

For the normative specifications this narrative paraphrases:

- [ADR-092 — Active Governance](/docs/adr/adr-092-active-governance.html) — the control-plane/data-plane boundary, provider-incorporation contract, and L0–L4 actuation ladder that position CyberArk as a governed provider rather than a competing control plane.
- [ADR-068 — Certificate-Based Authentication for Privileged Accounts](/docs/adr/adr-068-cba-privileged-accounts.html) — the requirement that PIM-eligible role activation requires CBA before elevation is granted.
- [OrgPath Codebook](/customer-documents/reference-architecture/codebook.html) — the fifteen-facet Model C schema that drives activation policy scoping throughout this book.
- [Architecture Decision Records](/docs/adr/index.html) — the binding record; this book is governed primarily by ADR-092, ADR-068, ADRs 051–056, and the CyberArk vendor overlay.
